title: Homa: The End of TCP for AI Clusters — John Ousterhout, Stanford
talk_summary: Ousterhout argues AI workloads are shifting from large throughput-bound transfers to small latency-bound message exchanges (KV-cache lookups, barrier sync, agentic coordination), where TCP/RDMA suffer high tail latency from incast and sender-side congestion control. He presents Homa, a message-based RPC protocol with receiver-driven congestion control, SRPT short-message prioritization, and switch priority queues, claiming ~13x better P99 for short messages.

takeaways.technique: Prioritize short control messages over bulk transfers in internal RPC
takeaways.what_they_do: Homa makes messages independent (not a byte stream) and uses SRPT plus switch priority queues so short coordination messages bypass queued bulk data instead of head-of-line blocking behind it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: shorter messages can bypass long ones, so they don't get queued behind long messages
takeaways.numbers: P99 short-message latency ~13x faster than TCP; long messages ~2x better

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of senders guessing rates from one-bit congestion signals, the receiver knows how much is coming and grants senders permission to send in chunks, delaying grants to avoid queue buildup.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the receiver has way more information ... it can therefore respond to congestion much more quickly and much more precisely

takeaways.what_they_do: Homa favors short messages via SRPT so small tasks complete fast rather than waiting behind large ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It uses SRPT, shortest remaining processing time first, to try and prioritize shorter messages
